title: Behavioral and Topological Heterogeneities in Network Versions of Schelling's Segregation Model

key_points.claim: Combining heterogeneous preferences with heterogeneous network topology yields reduced segregation and richer outcomes.
key_points.evidence_quote: with concurrent increased representations of heterogeneous preferences and heterogeneous topologies, reduced levels of segregation emerge.

key_points.claim: New dynamic: tolerant agents occupy dense areas and push intolerant agents to sparse areas, resembling an urban-rural divide.
key_points.evidence_quote: highly tolerant nodes take residence in dense areas and push intolerant nodes to sparse areas mimicking the urban-rural divide.

key_points.claim: Prior work: heterogeneous preferences reduce segregation, but heterogeneous topology alone does not; no earlier study combined both.
key_points.evidence_quote: No previous studies of combined dimensions of heterogeneity were identified.

key_points.claim: Method: simulations on 2D lattices with varying densification to create clusters and hubs, comparing homogeneous and heterogeneous preference models.
key_points.evidence_quote: Simulations were conducted using both homogeneous and heterogeneous preference models on 2D lattices with varied levels of densification

key_points.claim: Framing: segregation is treated as emerging from individual preferences (Schelling/Sakoda tradition), and is relevant to legal debate on de facto versus de jure segregation.
key_points.evidence_quote: segregation is an emergent property arising from the collective dynamics of individuals and their choices in mostly-free housing markets.

reliability_notes: Full text was fetched, but I only read the abstract and introduction (the first ~5,000 characters). The paper is an arXiv preprint and may not be peer reviewed. It covers one narrow topic, residential segregation ABMs on networks.
